formula_checks.name: benefitActiveMonths
formula_checks.why: Selects the recorded payment months; all twelve when none is named is an explicit planning convention, not confirmation of receipts.
formula_checks.rests_on: Written purpose and formula, on the stated valid input domain; ordinary arithmetic

formula_checks.name: benefitAnnual
formula_checks.why: Monthly amount times the confirmed/planned active-month count; no annualizing a seasonal benefit to twelve months.
formula_checks.rests_on: Written purpose and formula, on the stated valid input domain; ordinary arithmetic

formula_checks.name: extraIncome
formula_checks.why: A supposedly one-time payment with no year recurs every year; missing timing is treated as recurring income. General taxability also needs source-specific classification.
formula_checks.should_be: Require a year for a one-time item; keep it pending if absent. Preserve actual payment month and source tax treatment.

formula_checks.name: currentRetirementIncomeMonthly
formula_checks.why: Honors an explicit deselection of current retirement income; the conversion is delegated without adding withdrawals to guaranteed outside income.
formula_checks.rests_on: Written purpose and formula, on the stated valid input domain; ordinary arithmetic

formula_checks.name: otherIncomeMonth
formula_checks.why: Uses the explicit January default and valid 1–12 calendar month range. This month helper does not establish a missing one-time year.
formula_checks.rests_on: Written purpose and formula, on the stated valid input domain; ordinary arithmetic

formula_checks.name: tipsAnnual
formula_checks.why: Counts months in which either earner has any salary; a tipped earner’s employment months can differ from the household’s.
formula_checks.should_be: Associate tips with the correct earner and paid months; retain the current result only for an explicitly household-wide monthly tip input.

formula_checks.name: retirementIncomeMonthly
formula_checks.why: Correct monthly conversion of the stated payment amounts. This arithmetic alone does not prove all streams taxable or guaranteed.
formula_checks.rests_on: Written purpose and formula, on the stated valid input domain; ordinary arithmetic

formula_checks.name: guaranteedOutsideStreams
formula_checks.why: Includes only the four owner-approved outside stream kinds, excluding withdrawals/RMDs and preserving an explicit inflation choice.
formula_checks.rests_on: Written purpose and formula, on the stated valid input domain; ordinary arithmetic

formula_checks.name: scholarshipByCalendarMonth
formula_checks.why: Places annual awards in their named months and monthly awards every month, rather than averaging a dated award.
formula_checks.rests_on: Written purpose and formula, on the stated valid input domain; ordinary arithmetic

formula_checks.name: incomeMonthlyGrid
formula_checks.why: The take-home identity is coherent on complete inputs, but it inherits the part-year wage-share error, undated recurring one-offs and yearless equity allocation.
formula_checks.should_be: Fix the dated readers first, then recombine gross, tax and 401(k) with identical scope on every screen.

rules_held.why: Year-month preservation is present in canonical wage tables,but annualized/converted paths and yearless vest/one-time defaults lose the same dated meaning.
rules_held.decision_in_force:
When you enter a year of income, the app asks which twelve months you mean — the calendar year, or the next twelve months from now. Three decisions:
1. Every month you enter carries its own month AND year, so entering across a New Year does not overwrite the wrong month.
2. Both ways of asking write to the same twelve calendar slots underneath, so the answer means the same thing however it was entered.
3. When a receipt is scanned, the total is read from the total — never from a line about how it was paid, which is not what you spent.

rules_held.decision_in_force:
The whole income surface redesigned. Six decisions:
1. Base pay becomes a full screen with one expandable section per earner — gross, 401(k), employer match, and what actually lands.
2. A 14-month dated table when pay varies, rather than one typical figure.
3. BOTH earners are captured, not one: a household on $84,000 plus $54,000 was being read as $84,000 — one person’s income against two people’s spending.
4. A filing-status question, which had never been asked, so every couple was taxed as a single filer.
5. Bonus and company shares follow the same who-earns pattern.
6. Interest and dividends are worked out from your holdings rather than asked for, and treated as TAXABLE BUT NOT SPENDABLE.
